# Chronic venous disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Vascular diseases > Chronic venous disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/gh0FWf)

---

## Summary

Chronic venous disease (also referred to as chronic venous disorders) is an umbrella term for a variety of clinical manifestations caused by chronically increased venous pressure in the lower extremities. Depending on the severity of hemodynamic dysfunction, manifestations can include <u>superficial</u> dilated <u>veins</u> (including <u>varicose veins</u>), <u>peripheral edema</u>, <u>skin</u> changes (e.g., <u>stasis dermatitis</u>), and <u>venous ulcers</u>. Diagnosis is based on clinical features and <u>duplex ultrasonography</u>, which shows vascular reflux and/or obstruction. Advanced diagnostic studies, such as <u>magnetic resonance venography</u> (<u>MRV</u>), may be indicated for certain patients. Treatment is aimed at reducing underlying venous <u>hypertension</u>. Lifestyle changes and localized vascular compression therapy are indicated for all patients. Surgical intervention is additionally recommended for patients with advanced or refractory disease. Surgical procedures are typically minimally invasive (e.g., endovenous <u>ablation</u>), although <u>vein</u> removal or <u>valvuloplasty</u> may be required. <u>Phlebotonic supplements</u>, most of which are available as nutritional supplements in the US, may help relieve symptoms such as <u>pain</u> and the sensation of heaviness.

---

## Definitions

* Venous insufficiency: disturbance in venous outflow; may be congenital (e.g., congenital absence of valves, <u>Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome</u>) or acquired (e.g., valvular injury secondary to <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>) [[1]](/library/xd1EHf0)

* Chronic venous disease/disorders (<u>CVD</u>): a spectrum of disorders caused by venous dysfunction; ranges from <u>telangiectasia</u> to venous <u>ulceration</u>

* Chronic venous insufficiency (<u>CVI</u>): advanced <u>CVD</u> including <u>edema</u>, <u>skin</u> changes, and venous <u>ulceration</u>

* Varicose veins: a type of <u>CVD</u> characterized by cylindrical dilation;  (diameter > 3 mm) and <u>tortuosity</u> of <u>superficial veins</u>





> [!TIP]
> The terms <u>CVD</u> and <u>CVI</u> are sometimes used interchangeably in literature because the pathophysiology is similar. However, most guideline definitions limit the term <u>CVI</u> to more advanced disease. [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>

* <u>CVI</u> affects 2–6% of women and ∼ 2% of men. [[5]](/library/YwXnhZ0)

* <u>Varicose veins</u> affect approx. 23% of individuals in the US. [[6]](/library/bwXHhZ0)

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (∼ 2:1)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

<u>Risk factors</u> for <u>CVD</u> include the following: : [[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)




* Increasing age and female sex

* <u>Family history</u> of venous disease

* Ligamentous laxity

* Sedentary lifestyle and prolonged standing

* <u>Obesity</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* Smoking

* Prior <u>deep vein thrombosis</u> (<u>DVT</u>) causing postthrombotic syndrome

* Prior extremity trauma

* Congenital abnormalities

---

## Pathophysiology

In healthy individuals, blood from the <u>superficial</u> <u>veins of the leg</u> passes through the <u>perforating veins</u> into the <u>deep veins</u>.




* Pathophysiology of <u>varicose veins</u>: elevated venous pressure (see “<u>Risk factors</u>” above) → <u>incompetence</u> of venous valves (<u>superficial</u> or <u>deep veins</u>) → reflux of blood into <u>superficial veins</u> and back into the extremity → further elevation of venous pressure → formation of <u>varicose veins</u>

* Pathophysiology of <u>CVI</u>: <u>varicose veins</u> → extravasation of protein and <u>leukocytes</u> → release of <u>free radicals</u> → damage to <u>capillary</u> <u>basement membrane</u> → leakage of <u>plasma proteins</u> → <u>edema</u> formation → ↓ oxygen supply → tissue <u>hypoperfusion</u> and <u>hypoxia</u> → inflammation and <u>atrophy</u> → possibly <u>ulcer</u> formation

## Clinical features

The following are all features of venous <u>hypertension</u>:




* Generalized or localized <u>pain</u>, lower extremity discomfort/cramping, and limb swelling

* Worsened by heat

* Worse while standing, relieved by walking and raising of legs

* <u>Pruritus</u>, tingling, and numbness

* <u>Edema</u> (may be unilateral) that starts in the ankle and may involve the calf later in the disease course (in about half of affected individuals)

* <u>Telangiectasias</u>

* Yellow-brown or red-brown <u>skin</u> pigmentation of the <u>medial</u> ankle; later of the foot and possibly lower leg

* <u>RBC breakdown</u> leads to <u>hemosiderin</u> release → accumulation in the <u>dermis</u> → <u>skin</u> pigmentation

* May lead to <u>stasis dermatitis</u>; a scaly, pruritic <u>rash</u>

* Paraplantar <u>varicose veins</u>

* Lipodermatosclerosis: Localized <u>chronic inflammation</u> and <u>fibrosis</u> of <u>skin</u> and subcutaneous tissues of lower leg [[7]](/library/jba_tQ)

* Painful, indurated, and hardened <u>skin</u>

* Atrophie blanche: white, coin- to palm-sized <u>atrophic</u> <u>plaques</u> due to absent <u>capillaries</u> in the <u>fibrotic</u> tissue

### <u>Tourniquet</u> tests for <u>varicose veins</u>




Bedside <u>tourniquet</u> tests may help determine the site of venous insufficiency, but imaging is required for diagnostic confirmation. [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)




* Trendelenburg test: evaluates the function of <u>superficial</u> and perforating venous valves [[6]](/library/bwXHhZ0)

* Perthes test: assesses deep venous patency  [[6]](/library/bwXHhZ0)[[8]](/library/Xi19Jg0)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Assess patients according to <u>CEAP classification</u>.

* Perform a thorough history and <u>clinical examination</u>.

* Obtain venous <u>duplex ultrasound</u> (US).

* Consider additional studies in consultation with vascular <u>surgery</u> if there is:

* Complicated disease

* Suspected suprainguinal venous obstruction  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* Diagnostic uncertainty

* Planned intervention

* Evaluate for concurrent <u>peripheral arterial disease</u> (<u>PAD</u>). 

* All patients: Check for pedal pulses. [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)

* Patients with <u>venous ulcers</u>  [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Measure <u>ankle-brachial index</u>.

* If ≤ 0.9, refer to a vascular specialist for <u>diagnostics for PAD</u>. [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)





### Venous <u>duplex ultrasound</u> [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)




* Indications: all patients with <u>varicose veins</u> or suspected <u>CVI</u>  [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)

* Characteristic findings

* Evidence of venous reflux  [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* <u>Ultrasound features of DVT</u> (acute or chronic) [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)





### Additional studies [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)




Not routinely required; consider in complications, diagnostic uncertainty, or planned interventions




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u>




* <u>CBC</u> and <u>BMP</u>: patients with <u>venous ulcers</u> [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)

* <u>Thrombophilia panel</u>: patients with <u>recurrent DVT</u>, <u>thrombosis</u> at a young age, or <u>thrombosis</u> in an atypical site (see also “<u>DVT diagnostics</u>”) [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)

* Microbiology : patients with venous <u>ulceration</u> and signs of active infection (see “<u>Complications of CVI</u>”)





#### Venous plethysmography (<u>venous function test</u>)




* A noninvasive test used to assess venous blood flow and detect reflux and/or obstruction

* Indications include quantification of reflux or obstruction if <u>duplex US</u> findings are unclear.  [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[12]](/library/a31QSg0)





#### Further imaging




* Abdominal/<u>pelvic</u> US: Consider as initial study for suspected suprainguinal venous obstruction. [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* CT or <u>MR venography</u>: Consider if <u>duplex US</u> is inconclusive and before planned intervention for suprainguinal venous obstruction.  [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* Invasive imaging (e.g., <u>contrast venography</u>, <u>intravascular</u> <u>ultrasound</u>): Consider if CT/<u>MRV</u> is inconclusive or inadequate. [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)





![Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)](media/u3nvuh7pxbdlyv8u3g0re1mz.jpg)

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Telangiectasia</u>

* Autoimmune disease, e.g., <u>CREST syndrome</u>

* Genetic causes, e.g., <u>hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia</u>

* <u>Spider telangiectasia</u> in <u>chronic liver disease</u> or <u>pregnancy</u>

* <u>Edema</u>: See “<u>Differential diagnoses of peripheral edema</u>.”

* <u>Skin</u> changes [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)

* <u>Cellulitis</u>

* <u>Allergic contact dermatitis</u>

* <u>Pigmented purpuric dermatosis</u>

* <u>Exercise-induced vasculitis</u>

* <u>Ulceration</u> [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* <u>Arterial ulcer</u>

* <u>Diabetic foot</u> wounds (<u>malum perforans</u>)

* <u>Pyoderma gangrenosum</u>

* Ulcerated <u>skin</u> tumors (e.g., <u>basal cell carcinoma</u>)

* <u>Pressure ulcer</u>

* <u>Vasculitis</u>

* Iliocaval venous obstruction  [[14]](/library/NDc-ee0)[[15]](/library/7Dc4fe0)





| <br>Differential diagnosis of leg ulcers<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br><u>Venous ulcer</u><br> | <br><u>Arterial ulcer</u><br> | <br><u>Malum perforans</u><br> |
| Location | <br>* <u>Gaiter region</u> (above the ankle)<br><br> | <br>* Pressure points of the foot and shin (e.g., <u>lateral malleolus</u>, tips of the toes)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Plantar</u> pressure points of the foot (over the heel or the head of the <u>metatarsal bones</u>)<br><br> |
| Mechanism | <br>* Chronic local venous <u>hypertension</u> leads to tissue <u>ischemia</u>.<br><br> | <br>* Vessel occlusion leads to tissue <u>ischemia</u>.<br><br> | <br>* Diabetic microvasculopathy and neuropathy leads to impaired tissue sustenance.<br><br> |
| Wound features | <br><br>* Irregular borders<br><br>* <u>Exudative</u><br><br>* <u>Superficial</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Punched-out appearance<br><br>* No exudation<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hyperkeratotic</u> borders<br><br>* Deep<br><br><br> |
| <u>Pain</u> | <br>* Mild<br><br> | <br>* Severe<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> |
| Additional features | <br><br>* <u>Varicose veins</u><br><br>* <u>Edema</u><br><br>* <u>Stasis dermatitis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Pale, shiny, cold, hairless surrounding <u>skin</u><br><br>* <u>Nail</u> <u>dystrophy</u><br><br>* Absent pulses<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Charcot joints</u><br><br>* Absent <u>ankle reflex</u><br><br>* Impaired sensation (esp. vibration)<br><br>* <u>Claw toes</u><br><br><br> |

## Treatment

### Approach [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)[[10]](/library/c_caMU0)




* All patients

* Identify and treat concomitant disease (e.g., <u>DVT</u>, <u>PAD</u>).

* Recommend lifestyle measures to improve <u>venous return</u> and prevent progression of <u>CVD</u>.

* Use the <u>revised venous clinical severity score</u> to assess treatment response.

* Symptomatic patients 

* Initiate compression therapy.

* Consider <u>phlebotonic supplements</u>.

* Symptomatic <u>varicose veins</u> and/or <u>edema</u> (<u>CEAP C2</u>/<u>CEAP C3</u>): Consider interventional therapies.

* <u>Skin</u> changes or <u>ulceration</u> (<u>CEAP C4</u>–C6): Refer to vascular <u>surgery</u> for interventional therapies.  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* See also “<u>Complications of CVI</u>” for further information on the management of <u>venous ulcers</u> and <u>stasis dermatitis</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Manage <u>CVD</u> in <u>pregnancy</u> with <u>conservative measures</u> only and reassess for persistent disease at 3–6 months after delivery. [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)




![Revised Venous Clinical Severity Score](media/t9dqxojry4ytf20w0x2tbrcm.jpg)

Revised Venous Clinical Severity Score




### Lifestyle modifications [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[10]](/library/c_caMU0)[[16]](/library/XwX9hZ0)




* Frequent elevation of the legs  [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Daily exercise  [[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)[[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)

* Change in footwear  [[17]](/library/2h1TWg0)

* Avoidance of:

* Long periods of standing and sitting

* Hot temperatures  [[18]](/library/Jh1sUg0)

* <u>Smoking cessation</u>

* <u>Management of obesity</u>

* <u>Emollients</u> to prevent dry <u>skin</u>  [[19]](/library/oh10Ug0)





> [!TIP]
> Consider referral to <u>physical therapy</u> to increase <u>calf pump activity</u> and help improve mobility. [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)




### Venous compression therapy




#### Indications [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[20]](/library/N-c-xU0)




* Primary treatment modality for:

* Most patients with symptomatic mild venous disease (<u>CEAP C1</u> or <u>CEAP C2</u>) or <u>edema</u>

* Pregnant patients with any stage of <u>CVD</u>

* Adjunct to interventional therapy: patients with <u>skin</u> changes or <u>ulceration</u> (<u>CEAP C4</u>–C6)





#### Contraindications [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)




* <u>PAD</u> with either:

* <u>ABI</u> < 0.6 (absolute) or < 0.8 (relative)  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Absolute ankle pressure < 60 mm Hg [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Prior peripheral arterial bypass grafting at the site of compression

* <u>NYHA</u> III and IV <u>congestive heart failure</u>

* Severe <u>diabetic neuropathy</u> or microangiopathy

* <u>Allergy</u> to <u>compression bandage</u> materials





> [!TIP]
> Active <u>ulceration</u> is not a contraindication to compression bandages; consult <u>wound care</u> to help manage concurrent wounds with compression dressings.




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid compression therapy in significant <u>PAD</u>.




#### Types of compression [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)




* Graded compression stockings 

* Options include below-the-knee, thigh-high, or waist-high products  [[21]](/library/Kh1UUg0)

* Can be applied by patients themselves

* Should be worn long-term all day, every day; adherence is often poor. [[22]](/library/ph1LUg0)

* Elasticity is lost over time; provide two pairs that should be alternated daily and replace after 6–9 months. [[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)

* Elastic or inelastic bandages (e.g., <u>Unna boots</u>) 

* Application of bandages requires trained staff.

* Multicomponent <u>elastic bandages</u> are the most effective form of compression therapy for <u>venous ulcers</u>.  [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Adjustable compression garments [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* Inelastic material with straps that can be tightened to increase pressure

* Used as an alternative to <u>compression stockings</u> or bandages

* <u>Intermittent pneumatic compression device</u>: for refractory <u>edema</u> or as a second-line option for <u>venous ulcers</u> [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)





> [!TIP]
> Some individuals (e.g., with <u>obesity</u> or limited mobility) may have difficulty applying compression garments and thus require a <u>donning</u> device or assistance. [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)

#### Amount of pressure [[4]](/library/tDcXTe0)




| <br>Recommended pressure for compression dressings in <u>CVD</u> [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Clinical condition | Pressure in mm Hg |
| <u>Varicose veins</u> | <br>* 15–30<br><br> |
| <u>Edema</u> or <u>skin</u> changes | <br>* 20–40<br><br> |
| <u>Postthrombotic syndrome</u> | <br>* 30–40  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)<br><br> |
| Active venous <u>ulceration</u> | <br>* 40–60  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)<br><br> |





### Interventional procedures




#### Indications [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[23]](/library/Ywcnhe0)




* Symptomatic <u>varicose veins</u> (<u>CEAP C2</u>) with:

* Known reflux in the <u>superficial venous system</u>  [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)

* A history of complications, e.g., bleeding, recurrent <u>superficial thrombophlebitis</u> [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[24]](/library/yh1dgg0)

* Unsuccessful <u>conservative management</u>

* <u>Edema</u> (<u>CEAP C3</u>): if other <u>causes of edema</u> are excluded and <u>conservative management</u> has failed  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* <u>Skin</u> changes or <u>ulceration</u> (<u>CEAP C4</u>–6)





#### Modalities




##### Management of venous reflux [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[23]](/library/Ywcnhe0)




* <u>Vein</u> <u>ablation therapies</u>: minimally invasive; typically preferred 

* First-line: <u>endovenous thermal ablation</u> (laser or radiofrequency)   [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* Alternative: chemical <u>ablation</u> (<u>sclerotherapy</u>)

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Partial or complete removal of a <u>vein</u>

* Ambulatory phlebectomy: removal of <u>superficial</u> <u>varicose veins</u> via small <u>incisions</u>

* Ligation with vein stripping: ligation of the saphenofemoral or <u>saphenopopliteal junction</u> and removal of the great and/or <u>small saphenous veins</u>

* <u>Vein</u> <u>valvuloplasty</u>: reconstruction of valves in the <u>deep veins</u> [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)





> [!WARNING]
> Before ablating or stripping <u>superficial veins</u>, confirm the <u>deep veins</u> are patent using <u>duplex US</u>.




##### Management of venous obstruction  [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)[[23]](/library/Ywcnhe0)




* First-line: endovascular recanalization and <u>stenting</u>

* Alternative: surgical reconstruction





### Phlebotonic supplements [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[10]](/library/c_caMU0)[[25]](/library/W31Phg0)




* <u>Venoactive drugs</u> that increase tone and/or decrease <u>capillary</u> permeability

* Consider as an adjunct therapy for patients with <u>pain</u> or <u>edema</u> secondary to <u>CVD</u>. [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)[[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* Examples include horse chestnut seed extract and micronized purified flavonoid fraction (e.g., diosmiplex).  [[26]](/library/n017g20)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Phlebotonics</u> may improve some <u>symptoms of CVI</u>, but there is a paucity of evidence on the <u>efficacy</u> and safety of long-term use. [[10]](/library/c_caMU0)

---

## Complications

### Stasis dermatitis [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)[[27]](/library/v-cA_U0)




* Definition: <u>eczematous dermatitis</u> of the lower extremities caused by chronic venous <u>hypertension</u> and inflammation

* Clinical features

* Poorly defined <u>erythematous</u>, <u>eczematous</u>, and sometimes scaly patches commonly involving the <u>medial malleolus</u>

* Can involve <u>pruritus</u>; scratching may cause <u>lichenification</u>.

* Acute <u>stasis dermatitis</u> can manifest with weeping, <u>vesicles</u>, and worsening <u>erythema</u> and <u>edema</u>.

* Diagnostics

* Perform <u>diagnostic studies for CVI</u>, including <u>duplex US</u>.

* Consider <u>skin biopsy</u> if there is diagnostic uncertainty. [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)

* Differential diagnosis: see “<u>Differential diagnosis of CVI</u>.”

* Treatment

* Initiate <u>treatment of CVI</u>, including compression therapy and referral for interventional treatment.

* Avoid harsh cleansers and regularly apply <u>emollients</u> (e.g., <u>petroleum jelly</u>).

* Advise patients to avoid scratching.  [[28]](/library/Dvc1Xe0)

* Identify and treat superimposed infections.  [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)

* Consider the following:

* Cold and/or wet compresses  [[29]](/library/fDckde0)

* Short-term use of <u>topical steroids</u> (e.g., <u>triamcinolone</u> acetonide 0.1% DOSAGE) for acute presentations or <u>pruritus</u> [[27]](/library/v-cA_U0)





> [!TIP]
> Treatment of <u>stasis dermatitis</u> includes addressing the underlying <u>CVI</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> Consider <u>antibiotic therapy for skin and soft tissue infections</u> only if there is strong suspicion for <u>cellulitis</u>. [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)[[27]](/library/v-cA_U0)[[30]](/library/4c13cf0)




![Advanced chronic venous insufficiency](media/lfjrs4jalla2svu246rwsha1.jpg)

Advanced chronic venous insufficiency




### Venous ulcers [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)[[14]](/library/NDc-ee0)[[31]](/library/MycMfU0)




* Definition: an open <u>skin</u> lesion of the leg or foot in an area affected by venous <u>hypertension</u> [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Etiology: usually caused by <u>CVI</u> with or without complications (e.g., untreated <u>stasis dermatitis</u>) [[13]](/library/iDcJVe0)

* Clinical features  [[32]](/library/211TTf0)

* Most frequently occurs just above the ankle (<u>gaiter region</u>)

* Manifests as a shallow <u>ulcer</u> with irregular borders

* Typically mild <u>pain</u> and <u>pruritus</u>

* Additional <u>clinical features of CVI</u> are usually present; , e.g., <u>edema</u>, <u>varicose veins</u>.

* Diagnostics [[14]](/library/NDc-ee0)

* Perform <u>diagnostic studies for CVI</u>.

* Perform <u>ABI</u> to rule out concurrent <u>PAD</u>.

* Work up as needed for important <u>differential diagnoses of leg ulcers</u> (e.g., with <u>diabetes screening</u>).

* Obtain aerobic and anaerobic wound cultures for suspected infections.

* Tissue <u>biopsy</u> is indicated for <u>ulcers</u> with any of the following :

* No signs of healing after being open continuously for 3 months or after 4–6 weeks of standard treatment

* Worsening despite treatment (e.g., worsening <u>pain</u>, increase in size)

* Atypical features

* Differential diagnosis: see “<u>Differential diagnoses of CVI</u>.” [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Treatment [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)[[14]](/library/NDc-ee0)[[31]](/library/MycMfU0)

* Initiate <u>treatment of CVI</u>, including compression therapy and referral for interventional treatment.

* Consider <u>pentoxifylline</u> DOSAGE to promote healing.  [[14]](/library/NDc-ee0)[[33]](/library/XCc9qe0)

* Provide topical <u>wound care</u>.

* Treat underlying <u>stasis dermatitis</u>. [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Consult <u>wound care</u> for <u>debridement</u> and dressing application.

* Other topical agents (e.g., <u>antiseptics</u>, <u>antibiotics</u>) are not recommended. [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)[[31]](/library/MycMfU0)

* Start systemic <u>antibiotics</u> if there is evidence of infection (e.g., <u>cellulitis</u>, <u>erysipelas</u>)

* Consider <u>skin graft</u> in large or refractory <u>ulcers</u>.

* Prognosis: Recurrence rate is as high as 70%. [[14]](/library/NDc-ee0)





> [!TIP]
> To prevent recurrence, compression therapy should be continued after a <u>venous ulcer</u> is healed. [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

### Other complications




* Complications of compression therapy

* Incorrect fitting can lead to <u>pain</u> and <u>skin</u> breakdown.   [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)

* <u>Contact dermatitis</u> [[11]](/library/rzcf8U0)

* Varicose vein hemorrhage 

* Elevate the leg and apply pressure to the bleeding site.

* If bleeding is heavy, initiate <u>management of hemorrhagic shock</u>.

* Intervention with <u>ablation</u> or <u>vein</u> ligation may be considered after bleeding is controlled. [[3]](/library/7zc48U0)

* <u>Superficial thrombophlebitis</u>  [[2]](/library/pzcLFU0)

* <u>DVT</u>  [[23]](/library/Ywcnhe0)





![Thigh-length compression stockings](media/kchs79wixvpaunm3kbi7ngom.jpg)
